q:
Source 1 (clinic pamphlet, 2015)
Adults at average risk should begin colorectal cancer screening at age 50. Good options include a colonoscopy every 10 years or an at-home stool test once a year. Talk with your health care provider about which test is right for you.
Source 2 (clinic pamphlet, 2024)
Colorectal cancer screening should now begin at age 45 for adults at average risk. A colonoscopy every 10 years and a yearly at-home stool test are both good choices. Ask your provider which test best fits your needs and health history. On which point do the two sources differ?
o: How often a person needs a colonoscopy
The age at which screening should begin
Whether an at-home stool test is a choice
Whether to ask a provider about which test
e: Source 1 says to start at age 50; Source 2 says to start at 45.
Both sources give the same test choices and timing and both say to talk with a provider.
t: Notice the word "now" in Source 2. It signals that the advice changed. Check the dates when sources disagree.
w: Both say a colonoscopy every 10 years.
Both list a yearly at-home stool test.
Both tell readers to ask their provider.

q:
A school nurse is writing a newsletter for parents of high school students about how much sleep teens need. Source 1 (statement from a national sleep medicine organization)
Teenagers ages 13 to 18 should sleep 8 to 10 hours in every 24-hour period on a regular basis. Getting less than this is linked to trouble paying attention, poor grades, low mood, and more injuries. Schools and families can help by protecting time for sleep.
Source 2 (article in a popular health magazine; sample text)
Most adults need at least 7 hours of sleep each night, says Dr. Ellen Park, a family physician who has written about health for 20 years. "People treat sleep as optional," she says, "but cutting it short raises the risk of high blood pressure and weight gain." Which source is more useful and credible for the nurse's purpose, and why?
o: Source 2, because a physician with 20 years of experience wrote it
Both are equally useful, because experts wrote both of them
Source 2, because it names specific diseases linked to poor sleep
Source 1, because sleep experts wrote it about teens specifically
e: Source 1 comes from sleep specialists and gives a figure for ages 13 to 18, exactly the nurse's audience.
Source 2 may be reliable, but it is about adults, so its 7-hour figure would understate what teens need.
t: Credible AND relevant: ask who wrote it, and whether it is about the people you are writing about.
w: The doctor is credible, but she is writing about adults, not teenagers.
Expert authors are not enough; the source also has to fit the topic, and Source 2 does not cover teens.
Specific details don't help if they describe the wrong age group.

q:
A student is researching how cigarette ads of the 1950s tried to make smoking seem safe. Source 1 (text of a magazine ad printed in 1954; sample text)
Feel fresh, feel calm, feel your best. Smooth Valley cigarettes are so mild and gentle on your throat that even busy doctors enjoy one after a long day at the hospital. Treat yourself to the smooth taste that doctors trust. Reach for a Smooth Valley today!
Source 2 (history article published in 2016)
In the 1940s and 1950s, tobacco companies often filled their ads with pictures of doctors and words like "mild" and "gentle" to suggest that their cigarettes were safe. These claims became much harder to defend after the 1964 Surgeon General's report linked smoking to lung cancer. Which statement about these sources is accurate for the student's research?
o: Source 1 is primary, since the ad itself comes from the period studied.
Source 2 is the primary source, because its facts about smoking are accurate.
Source 1 cannot be a primary source, because its health claims are false.
Both are secondary sources, because neither one was written by a smoker.
e: The student is studying the ads themselves, so an actual 1954 ad is original evidence: a primary source.
Source 2 was written decades later and explains the ads, so it is secondary. A primary source can be biased or wrong and still be primary.
t: Primary = created at the time, as part of the thing you're studying. It can still be biased.
w: Accuracy does not make a source primary; Source 2 is a later account written about the period.
Primary means first-hand evidence from the time, not truthful. A misleading ad is exactly what this student needs to examine.
Primary status depends on when and how a source was created, not on whether a smoker wrote it.

q:
Source 1 (from a booklet for children with diabetes)
Sometimes your blood sugar can drop too low. You might feel shaky, sweaty, dizzy, or grumpy. If that happens, stop what you are doing and tell a grown-up right away. Then eat or drink your fast sugar snack, like juice or glucose tabs. You did the right thing!
Source 2 (from a school district guideline)
If a student shows signs of hypoglycemia or has a blood glucose below 70 mg/dL, give 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, such as 4 ounces of juice. Recheck the glucose in 15 minutes and repeat the treatment if it is still below 70 mg/dL. Notify the parent and document the event. How do the purpose and audience of the two sources differ?
o: Source 1 is for parents and explains insulin doses; Source 2 is for students.
Source 1 warns children to avoid sugar; Source 2 tells staff to limit snacks.
Source 1 helps kids spot a low and get help; Source 2 gives staff steps.
Both are for school staff, but Source 2 uses more technical medical words.
e: Source 1 uses simple, encouraging words ("tell a grown-up," "You did the right thing!") so a child can recognize a low and ask for help.
Source 2 uses exact numbers (70 mg/dL, 15 grams, 15 minutes) and tasks like documenting, so it is written for the adults who treat the student.
t: Who is "you"? Word choice and level of detail reveal the intended reader.
w: Source 1 speaks to the child ("tell a grown-up") and never mentions insulin.
Both sources tell the reader to USE sugar to treat a low, not avoid it.
Source 1 talks directly to a child, not to staff.

q:
Source 1 (from a skin cancer prevention fact sheet)
Use a broad-spectrum sunscreen with an SPF of 30 or higher on all skin that clothing will not cover. Apply it about 15 minutes before you go outside. Reapply at least every two hours, and more often if you are sweating or swimming.
Source 2 (from a farm safety flyer for field crews)
Long days in the sun add up. Protect yourself with a wide-brimmed hat and a lightweight, long-sleeved shirt, and take shade breaks whenever you can. If you use sunscreen, put more on every two hours, because sweat wears it off during field work. On which point do both sources agree?
o: Sunscreen should be put on again about every two hours.
Sunscreen should have an SPF of 30 or higher.
A wide-brimmed hat protects the skin better than sunscreen does.
Workers should take breaks in the shade.
e: Source 1 says to reapply "at least every two hours," and Source 2 says to "put more on every two hours."
w: Neither source compares hats with sunscreen.

q:
At Thursday's meeting, a parent asked the staff at Westfield Elementary to send nurse-visit notes home by text message instead of on paper slips. Many slips never reach parents, she said, because they get lost in backpacks, and some parents do not hear about a bump on the head until days later. The office manager disagreed. "We have sent paper slips home with children for as long as this school has existed," she said. "Our families are used to it, and there is no reason to change a system that has served us for forty years."

Which flaw appears in the office manager's reasoning?
o: She attacks the parent instead of answering her point.
She assumes a practice is good just because it is old.
She draws a broad conclusion from one lost paper slip.
She claims that one change will lead to a chain of bad events.
e: Saying "we have always done it this way" is an appeal to tradition: how long a habit has lasted is not evidence that it works.
She never answers the parent's actual point, that many slips never reach home.
t: "We've always done it" tells you how long, not how well.
w: She says nothing about the parent herself; she just defends the old system.
The parent's point is about many lost slips, and the manager does not generalize from any example.
She predicts no chain of events; she only says the system is long-standing.

q:
Free anatomy tutoring is offered in the campus library, but few nursing students use it. Nursing students spend most of their time between classes in the lounge of the health sciences building, and the library is a ten-minute walk from there. The college should move anatomy tutoring into the lounge. If tutors were right where nursing students already gather, many more of them would get the help they need to pass.

The argument depends on which unstated assumption?
o: Anatomy is the hardest course in the nursing program.
The library tutors are not well trained in anatomy.
The lounge is a quieter place to study than the library.
The walk is a main reason students skip tutoring now.
e: The plan only works if location is what keeps students away. If they skip tutoring because of the hours or their jobs, moving it will not help.
Test an assumption by denying it: if the walk does not matter, the conclusion falls apart.
t: Negation test: deny the choice. If the argument collapses, you found the assumption.
w: The argument is about where tutoring happens; it works whether or not anatomy is the hardest course.
The argument needs the opposite: it takes for granted that the tutors can help, so poorly trained tutors would hurt the plan, not support it.
The author never says the lounge is quieter; the point is that students are already there.

q:
A wellness website promotes CleanStart herbal tea with this paragraph: "CleanStart is the most effective detox tea you can buy. People who drink it get better detox results than they get from any other tea on the market, and that is exactly what makes it the most effective. When a tea outperforms every other product, you can trust that it is the best. Try CleanStart for 30 days and feel the difference for yourself."

What is the main problem with the reasoning in this paragraph?
o: It relies on the story of a single satisfied customer.
It compares the tea to something very different from it.
Its reason just repeats its claim in other words.
It assumes that any herbal product must be safe.
e: "Gets better results than any other tea" means the same thing as "most effective." The paragraph gives no test, data, or comparison, only the claim restated.
This is circular reasoning: the conclusion is used as its own support.
t: Circular check: cover the conclusion. Is any reason left that doesn't just say the same thing again?
w: No customer story is given; the paragraph names no one at all.
The tea is compared only with other teas, which is not a mismatched comparison; the problem is that no evidence is given.
Safety is never discussed; the problem is how the paragraph supports its claim about effectiveness.

q:
Fast-food restaurants serve hundreds of customers an hour because every worker does one simple task over and over: one takes orders, one cooks, and one bags the food. Our emergency department should work the same way. If one nurse did nothing but take blood pressures, another did nothing but start IVs, and a third did nothing but give medicines, every patient would move through the department as quickly as a lunch order.

Why is the comparison in this argument weak?
o: ER patients need very different care; lunch orders are nearly identical.
Restaurant workers and nurses are both paid by the hour for their shifts.
The argument never says how many nurses work in the department each shift.
Fast-food restaurants are often criticized for serving food that is unhealthy.
e: An analogy is only as strong as the likeness that matters. Fast food is quick because orders are standardized, but ER patients differ widely and their needs change quickly.
A crash victim, a feverish infant, and a stroke patient cannot be handled like identical burgers.
t: False analogy: ask whether the two things are alike in the way the argument needs.
w: This is a similarity, and it has nothing to do with whether an assembly-line method would work.
Staffing numbers are a minor detail; the flaw is that the two situations differ in the way that matters.
True or not, food quality is off topic; the argument is about speed of service.

q:
A parent group is urging the school board to ban all peanut products from district campuses. Their letter quotes Dr. Rosa Medina, a pediatric allergist at a Fresno children's hospital, who notes that peanuts are among the most common causes of severe food reactions in children. The letter also quotes Dr. Medina's view that a ban would cost the district little, because food vendors could switch to other snacks without raising lunch prices.

Which statement best evaluates the letter's use of Dr. Medina as an expert?
o: She is a reliable source on both points, because she is a doctor.
She is unreliable on both points, because a group that wants a ban quotes her.
She is a reliable source on the ban's cost but not on the allergy facts.
She is a strong source on allergies but not on vendor costs.
e: Expertise counts only within the expert's field. An allergist is a strong source on how common and serious peanut allergy is.
Whether vendors can switch snacks without raising prices is a question of school budgets and food contracts, which is outside her training.
t: Match the expert to each claim separately. One letter can use the same person well and badly.
w: A medical degree does not make someone an expert on food-service contracts and pricing.
Being quoted by one side does not cancel her expertise; the allergy facts are squarely in her field.
This reverses it: allergy facts are her field, and vendor pricing is not.

q:
(1) Last spring, the Riverside High cafeteria began offering a free salad bar at lunch. (2) Students who used the salad bar said they were eating more vegetables than before. (3) The district should therefore add salad bars at all of its high schools. (4) In addition, the district's produce supplier has offered to deliver to every school at no extra charge.

What role does sentence 4 play in the argument?
o: It states the argument's main conclusion.
It gives another reason for the conclusion.
It raises an objection the author must answer.
It gives background with no bearing on the claim.
e: Sentence 3, signaled by "therefore," is the conclusion. Sentence 4 begins "In addition" and gives one more reason to accept it: the plan would not raise delivery costs.
A conclusion is not always the last sentence; look for signal words such as therefore, so, and thus.
t: Conclusion signals: therefore, so, thus. Reason signals: because, since, in addition.
w: The last sentence is not always the conclusion; "therefore" marks sentence 3 as the claim.
Free delivery helps the author's case; it is not a point against it.
Free delivery makes the plan cheaper, so it does bear on whether the district should do it.

q:
Last fall, water refill stations were installed at three Modesto middle schools. In the months that followed, the school stores at those campuses sold about one-third fewer sugary drinks. Students told the school nurses that they liked filling their bottles with cold, free water between classes. Each station cost the district less than a single classroom computer, and the custodians report that the stations need very little upkeep.

Which sentence would best conclude this argument?
o: Sugary drinks are the main reason that Modesto children get cavities.
Students should be required to carry a full water bottle to every class.
The district should consider refill stations at its other schools.
School stores at every school should stop selling all drinks right away.
e: A good conclusion follows from all the evidence without going beyond it: the stations were cheap, popular, and linked to fewer sugary-drink sales.
Considering stations at other schools is a reasonable next step that the evidence supports.
t: Pick the conclusion that all the evidence supports without going further: watch for new topics, requirements, and bans.
w: The passage never discusses cavities; this brings in a new, unsupported claim.
The evidence shows students used the stations by choice; it does not support a requirement.
Too extreme: the evidence supports adding water, not banning every drink.

q:
Ms. Vang's son had a fever of 101 °F on Monday night. She wants to know when he may go back to school. Source 1 (from a district student health policy; sample text)
Students with a fever of 100.0 °F or higher must stay home. A student may return after being fever-free for 24 hours without the use of fever-reducing medicine such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen. Contact the school nurse with any questions.
Source 2 (from a children's health magazine)
A fever is one of the body's ways of fighting infection. Most fevers in children are caused by viruses and go away on their own within a few days. Keep your child comfortable, offer plenty of fluids, and call the doctor if the fever lasts more than three days. Which source better answers Ms. Vang's question, and why?
o: Source 1, because it states when a student may return to class
Source 2, because it explains what causes most fevers in children
Source 2, because it says when to call the doctor about a fever
Both equally, because both sources are about children's fevers
e: Her question is about returning to school, and only Source 1 gives the rule: 24 hours fever-free without fever-reducing medicine.
Source 2 offers useful home-care advice, but it never mentions school.
t: Underline the exact question first, then find the source that answers that question, not just the same topic.
w: True, but the cause of a fever does not tell her when he can go back to school.
Knowing when to call a doctor is different from knowing the school's return rule.
Sharing a topic is not enough; only one source answers her exact question.

q:
Source 1 (Hillcrest High student newspaper; sample text)
Vaping is far more common at Hillcrest than adults realize. In an anonymous online survey completed by 610 of the school's 900 students, 21 percent said they had vaped at least once in the past month. Several students we interviewed said vaping happens mostly off campus, at parties and on weekends, where no teacher sees it.
Source 2 (principal's report to the school board; sample text)
Vaping is a minor problem at Hillcrest. School records show that only 14 students, under 2 percent of enrollment, were sent to the office for vaping on campus last year. With new vape detectors in the restrooms and more staff watching the hallways, our campus remains a healthy place to learn. What best explains why the two sources reach different conclusions?
o: Source 2 includes every student, so its count is the more complete one.
The sources disagree about how many students attend the high school.
They use different data: self-reports vs. students caught at school.
A student newspaper's survey can't be trusted, so Source 1 is wrong.
e: Source 1 relies on students' anonymous reports of their own behavior; Source 2 counts only students caught vaping on campus, which misses everyone who is not caught.
Different data lead to different conclusions. Neither source has to be lying, but Source 2's measure is likely to undercount.
t: When sources disagree, compare HOW each one measured before deciding who is right.
w: The 900 is enrollment, but Source 2 counts only the 14 students actually caught, which is far from complete.
Both describe the same school: 14 students is under 2 percent of 900, which fits Source 1's enrollment figure.
Who publishes a survey does not make it false; an anonymous survey of 610 students is reasonable data.

q:
Source 1 (flyer from a sports-drink company, handed out at a youth soccer clinic; sample text)
Every drop of sweat carries away electrolytes your muscles need. PowerPlay sports drink puts them back, so young athletes stay strong from the first whistle to the last. Coaches across the Valley trust PowerPlay. Grab a bottle before every practice!
Source 2 (from a pediatric nutrition fact sheet)
For most children who play for less than an hour, plain water is all they need. Sports drinks contain added sugar and extra calories, and drinking them often can contribute to weight gain and tooth decay. They may help during long, intense exercise in hot weather. Which information does Source 1 leave out, most likely because of its purpose?
o: That sweat carries electrolytes away from the muscles
That water alone is enough for most short practices
That sports drinks can help during long, hot workouts
That coaches in the area recommend the drink to players
e: The company wants children to buy a bottle before every practice, so it leaves out the fact that water is usually enough, along with the added sugar.
Source 2 has nothing to sell, so it includes those facts.
t: Ask what the writer wants you to do, then look for the facts that would make you less likely to do it.
w: Source 1 does say this; it is the flyer's main selling point.
This fact favors the product, so a seller would have no reason to hide it.
Source 1 includes this claim: "Coaches across the Valley trust PowerPlay."

q:
Rosa's insurance does not cover her blood pressure pill, so she pays cash. Her doctor sent a prescription for a 90-day supply. Rosa wants to pick up all 90 days at one time and pay the lowest price. She called four pharmacies near her home in Madera.
Cash price, lisinopril 10 mg (sample data)
Pharmacy30-day supply90-day supply
Valley Drug$12$30
Main Street Pharmacy$9$29
Central Discount Rx$14$24
Grove Pharmacy$10$27
Which pharmacy should Rosa choose?
e: Rosa needs the 90-day column. Its lowest price is $24, at Central Discount Rx.
Central Discount Rx has the HIGHEST 30-day price, which is why reading the right column matters.
t: Find the column that matches the question before you compare numbers.
w: Lowest 30-day price ($9), but its 90-day price is $29.
$30 for 90 days, the highest in that column.
$27 for 90 days, $3 more than Central Discount Rx.

q:
From a hospital newsletter: "This year our budget is $200 million. More than half of it goes to the nurses, doctors and other staff who care for patients. The chart shows how the whole budget is divided."

Based on the newsletter and the chart, about how much did the hospital budget for supplies and medicines?
e: The chart shows supplies and medicines at 20%, and the text gives the total: $200 million.
20% of $200 million = 0.20 × 200 = $40 million.
t: A pie chart gives shares; the text gives the whole. You need both to get dollars.
w: That is the percentage (20) read as millions of dollars, not 20% of $200 million.
That is the staff share: 54% of $200 million.
That is the staff percentage (54) read as millions of dollars.

q:
The surgical unit keeps one nurse on call each weeknight to come in for emergency cases. If the on-call nurse is sick, the charge nurse calls that night's backup nurse instead of choosing someone else.
On-call schedule, week of March 9 (sample data)
NightOn callBackup
MonKimLee
TueNguyenKim
WedLeePatel
ThuPatelOrtiz
FriOrtizNguyen
Patel calls in sick on Thursday. Whom should the charge nurse call?
e: Find Thursday's row: Patel is on call and Ortiz is the backup.
The text says to call that night's backup, so the answer is Ortiz.
w: Lee is on call Wednesday, the row above Thursday.
Nguyen is Friday's backup, not Thursday's.
Kim works Monday and Tuesday, not Thursday.

q:
A pediatric clinic guideline says a baby's weight needs a closer look if, compared with an earlier visit, it falls across two or more of the major percentile lines on the growth chart. The major lines are the 95th, 90th, 75th, 50th, 25th, 10th and 5th.
Baby Leo's weight-for-age percentile (sample data)
Age2 mo4 mo6 mo9 mo12 mo
Percentile80th72nd60th45th30th
Compared with the 2-month visit, at which visit does Leo's weight FIRST meet the guideline for a closer look?
e: From the 80th percentile, Leo drops below the 75th line at 4 months. He stays above the 50th line until 9 months.
At 9 months (45th), he has crossed two major lines, the 75th and the 50th, so 9 months is the first visit that qualifies.
t: Count the lines crossed, not the points dropped.
w: 80th to 72nd crosses only one line, the 75th.
A 20-point drop, but 60th is still above the 50th line, so only one line (75th) is crossed.
The 30th still crosses only two lines (75th and 50th), and it is not the FIRST visit to do so.

q:
To keep patients who may be contagious away from others, front-desk staff at a Visalia clinic follow the check-in steps below for every patient. The steps work like a flowchart. A patient arrives and says, "I've had a bad cough since yesterday."
Check-in steps
StepAction
1Ask: "Do you have a fever or a new cough?" If yes, go to step 2. If no, go to step 4.
2Give the patient a mask.
3Seat the patient in Waiting Area B. Go to step 5.
4Seat the patient in Waiting Area A.
5Take vital signs when the patient is called back.
Which steps apply to this patient, in order?
e: A "yes" at step 1 sends the patient to step 2 (mask), then step 3 (Area B).
Step 3 says "Go to step 5," so step 4 is skipped.
t: In a flowchart, the "go to" directions matter more than the numbers.
w: Step 3 sends the patient to step 5; reading straight down misses the "go to" direction.
That is the path for a patient who answers "no" at step 1.
Step 4 is Waiting Area A, for patients without fever or cough.

q:
A health columnist wrote that asthma emergency visits in County B "have now caught up with" those in County A, and she urged County B to expand its asthma programs. The graph shows the yearly rate of asthma visits to emergency rooms in each county from 2019 to 2024.

Which statement about the graph is accurate?
o: County B's rate passed County A's rate by 2024.
County A's rate went up every year after 2019.
The gap shrank from 22 to 1 visit per 10,000.
Both counties' rates rose by about the same amount.
e: In 2019 the gap was 62 − 40 = 22; in 2024 it was 55 − 54 = 1.
County B nearly matched County A, so "caught up" is close, but B never passed A.
w: In 2024 County B (54) was still just below County A (55).
County A's rate fell every year, from 62 to 55.
County A fell by 7 while County B rose by 14; they moved in opposite directions.

q:
A sign at Valley Urgent Care says: "Average wait on Monday: 38 minutes." A patient deciding whether to come in wonders if that is how long she should expect to wait. Here are Monday's waits.
Monday's waits, check-in to exam room (sample data)
Patient123456789
Wait (min)1215141822216131715
Which statement best describes the posted average?
o: It is accurate and typical, since most patients waited close to 38 minutes.
It is too low, because one patient waited more than 3 hours.
It cannot be correct, because no patient waited exactly 38 minutes.
It is pulled up by one long wait; most patients waited under 20 minutes.
e: The waits add to 342 minutes; 342 ÷ 9 = 38, so the average is correct.
But one 222-minute wait drags it up. Eight of nine patients waited 12 to 18 minutes; the middle value is 15.
t: One extreme value can drag an average far from what is typical. Look for it.
w: No patient waited near 38 minutes; eight waited under 20 and one waited 222.
The long wait is already in the average; it pushes the average UP, not down.
An average does not have to equal any single value; 342 ÷ 9 really is 38.

q:
Marisol compared her family's monthly budgets after she got a raise. She said, "We're spending less on food now. It went from 30 percent of our budget down to 25 percent." Her husband asked to see the numbers before he agreed.
Marisol's monthly budget (sample data)
YearTake-home payHousingFoodEverything else
2024$3,00035%30%35%
2025$4,00035%25%40%
Which statement best evaluates Marisol's claim?
o: It is wrong; food rose from $900 to $1,000 a month.
It is right; a smaller percentage always means fewer dollars.
It is right, because the food share dropped by 5 percentage points.
It is wrong, because the food share rose from 25% to 30%.
e: Food took a smaller SHARE of a bigger paycheck, so the dollars spent on food went up by $100.
t: A percentage is only half the story. Multiply by the total to get dollars.
w: Not when the total grows: 25% of $4,000 is more than 30% of $3,000.
The share did drop, but that does not show fewer dollars; the total pay changed too.
Reversed: the share went from 30% in 2024 to 25% in 2025.

q: The ring-shaped molecule shown contains only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, in about a 1:2:1 ratio. To which class of macromolecules does it belong?
e: This is glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆). A formula with C, H and O in a 1:2:1 ratio, (CH₂O)ₙ, is the signature of a carbohydrate.
Glucose is a monosaccharide, the monomer for starch, glycogen and cellulose. It is the cell's main quick-energy fuel.
w: Proteins contain nitrogen in every amino acid.
Nucleic acids contain nitrogen and phosphorus.
Lipids have far less oxygen than a 1:2:1 ratio.
fig: Structure drawing from ItsDrDan's Carbohydrates game.

q: Many molecules like the one shown are linked together and stored in the liver and muscles to be used for quick energy later. What is that storage molecule called?
e: Animals store extra glucose as glycogen, a highly branched chain of glucose units, mainly in the liver and skeletal muscle.
When blood glucose drops, the hormone glucagon signals the liver to break glycogen back down into glucose.
Plants store glucose as starch. Cellulose is a plant fiber humans cannot digest.
w: Cellulose is in plant cell walls; humans can't digest it.
Keratin is a protein in hair and nails.
fig: Structure drawing from ItsDrDan's Carbohydrates game.

q: The molecule shown is made from glycerol and three fatty acids. What is it?
e: Tri- means three: a triglyceride has three fatty acid chains attached to one glycerol (the three-carbon backbone on the left).
A phospholipid has only TWO fatty acids; the third position holds a phosphate group.
w: A phospholipid has two fatty acids plus a phosphate group.
Polypeptides are chains of amino acids.
fig: Structure drawing from ItsDrDan's Lipids game.

q: In the triglyceride shown, which fatty acid chain is unsaturated?
e: An unsaturated fatty acid has at least one carbon–carbon double bond (C=C).
Only the bottom chain has "CH=CH" in it. The top and middle chains are all single bonds, (CH₂)ₙ, so they are saturated (full of hydrogen).
w: The top chain is (CH₂)₁₄CH₃: no double bonds.
The middle chain is (CH₂)₁₆CH₃: no double bonds.
The bottom chain has a CH=CH double bond.
fig: Structure drawing from ItsDrDan's Lipids game.

q: Fatty acid A is saturated and fatty acid B is unsaturated (cis). Why are fats made mostly of chains like A (such as butter) usually solid at room temperature, while oils made mostly of chains like B are liquid?
o: Straight chains like A pack tightly, so more heat is needed to melt them.
Chain A has more double bonds, which link neighboring molecules together.
Chain B is much longer, so its molecules slide past each other easily.
Chain B contains nitrogen atoms, which keep the oil molecules liquid.
e: A saturated chain (A) has only single bonds, so it is straight. Straight chains stack closely, like pencils in a box, and attract each other strongly, so the fat is solid at room temperature.
A cis double bond (B) puts a kink in the chain. Kinked chains can't pack tightly, so the attractions are weaker and the oil stays liquid.
Olive oil, which is mostly unsaturated, is liquid at room temperature. (Separately, diets high in saturated fat are linked to higher LDL cholesterol.)
w: A has NO double bonds; B has one.
Fatty acids contain only C, H and O.
fig: Structure drawing from ItsDrDan's Lipids game.

q: The molecule shown has a polar (water-loving) phosphate head and two nonpolar (water-fearing) fatty acid tails. What is its main job in the body?
o: Forming the double layer (bilayer) of cell membranes
Storing genetic information in the nucleus of each cell
Speeding up chemical reactions in the cytoplasm
Binding and carrying oxygen in red blood cells
e: This is a phospholipid. In water, phospholipids line up in two layers: heads face the watery inside and outside of the cell, and tails hide in the middle.
That phospholipid bilayer is the basic structure of every cell membrane.
fig: Structure drawing from ItsDrDan's Lipids game.

q: When the three amino acids in the figure were joined, what else was produced?
e: Each peptide bond forms by dehydration synthesis (condensation): an OH from one amino acid and an H from the next are removed as a water molecule.
Two peptide bonds → two water molecules. Breaking the bonds again (digestion) is hydrolysis, which uses water to split them.
w: One water per bond, and there are only two bonds.
No O₂ is made when monomers join.
CO₂ is made in cellular respiration, not when amino acids join.
fig: Structure drawing from ItsDrDan's Amino Acids game.

q: The figure shows a chain of amino acids in a specific order. Which level of protein structure is this?
e: Primary structure is the SEQUENCE of amino acids in the chain, like letters spelling a word.
The DNA code determines this order, and the order determines how the chain will fold.
w: Secondary structure is local folding (helix or sheet).
Tertiary is the whole 3-D fold of one chain.
Quaternary is two or more chains together.
fig: Structure drawing from ItsDrDan's Amino Acids game.

q: The figure shows a protein made of four separate polypeptide chains fitted together, like hemoglobin. Which level of protein structure is this?
e: Quaternary structure exists only when a protein is made of two or more polypeptide chains (subunits).
Hemoglobin has four: two α and two β chains, each holding an iron-containing heme group (the red squares).
w: Primary is the amino acid sequence.
Secondary is local folding like a helix.
Tertiary is the fold of ONE chain.

q: In the nucleotide shown, carbon 2 of the sugar has only H atoms (no OH group). Which nucleic acid would this nucleotide be part of?
o: DNA, because the sugar is deoxyribose
RNA, because the sugar is ribose
RNA, because the base is adenine
DNA, because it has a phosphate group
e: De-oxy-ribose means ribose missing an oxygen: it has H instead of OH on carbon 2. That sugar is found in DNA.
RNA's sugar, ribose, has an OH on carbon 2.
Adenine and phosphate groups are found in BOTH DNA and RNA, so they don't tell you which one it is.
w: Ribose has an OH on carbon 2.
Adenine is found in both DNA and RNA.
Both DNA and RNA nucleotides have phosphate.
fig: Structure drawing from ItsDrDan's Nucleic Acids game.

q: The top DNA strand reads 5′-A-T-G-C-3′. Reading the matching (complementary) strand under it from left to right, 3′ to 5′, what is its sequence?
e: In DNA, A pairs with T and G pairs with C (as shown on the ladder).
So A–T–G–C pairs with T–A–C–G.
U (uracil) replaces T only in RNA, so U–A–C–G would be the matching RNA strand made during transcription.
w: That's the same strand, not its partner.
U is found in RNA, not DNA.
That pairs A with C and T with G; DNA pairs A–T and G–C.
fig: Structure drawing from ItsDrDan's Nucleic Acids game.

q: According to the graph, at about what temperature does this human enzyme work best?
e: The highest point of the curve (optimum temperature) is at about 37 °C.
That is normal human body temperature, where most human enzymes work best.
w: At 50 °C activity has already fallen sharply.
At 70 °C the enzyme has no activity.
fig: Structure drawing from ItsDrDan's Enzyme game.

q: Based on the graph, why does the enzyme's activity drop so quickly above about 45 °C?
o: Heat changes the enzyme's shape (denatures it), so the substrate no longer fits.
The enzyme gets used up in each reaction, and heat makes it run out faster.
Molecules move more slowly at high temperature, so they collide less often.
Heat changes the substrate into a different molecule that the enzyme can no longer use.
e: Up to the optimum, warmth speeds molecules up and they collide more, so activity rises.
Past the optimum, heat breaks the bonds holding the enzyme's 3-D shape. The active site changes shape, the substrate no longer fits, and activity crashes.
This is one reason a very high fever is dangerous.
w: Enzymes are not used up; they are reused.
Molecules move FASTER when it's hotter.
The substrate is unchanged; the enzyme's shape is the problem.
fig: Structure drawing from ItsDrDan's Enzyme game.

q: Pepsin works in the stomach and trypsin works in the small intestine. Based on the graph, which statement is best supported?
o: The stomach is strongly acidic, and the small intestine is slightly basic.
Both organs have the same pH, so either enzyme could work in either organ.
Pepsin works best in a basic environment, so the stomach must be basic.
Trypsin would work well in the stomach because it digests protein too.
e: Pepsin's activity peaks at pH 2 (strongly acidic). That fits the stomach, where hydrochloric acid keeps the pH around 1.5–3.5.
Trypsin peaks at about pH 8 (slightly basic). In the small intestine, bicarbonate from the pancreas neutralizes stomach acid.
Trypsin has almost no activity at pH 2, so it would not work in the stomach.
w: Their best pH values are very different (2 vs 8).
Pepsin peaks at pH 2, which is acidic, and the stomach is acidic.
Trypsin has almost no activity at stomach pH.

q: The diagram shows the same reaction with and without an enzyme. What does the enzyme change?
o: It lowers the activation energy, so the reaction goes faster.
It lowers the energy of the products, so more energy is released.
It adds energy to the reactants so they can get over the hill.
It changes which products form, so a different reaction occurs.
e: The dashed green curve (with enzyme) has a lower hill. The enzyme lowers the activation energy, so many more molecules can react per second.
The starting and ending energy levels are the same on both curves, so the enzyme does not change the overall energy released or the products.
Enzymes are catalysts: they speed reactions and are not used up.
w: The products end at the same level on both curves, so the energy released is the same.
Enzymes don't add energy; they lower the barrier.
The products are the same; only the speed changes.

q: Use the table. Which macromolecule class do enzymes, antibodies and hemoglobin belong to?
e: Proteins do most of the work in cells: enzymes speed reactions, antibodies defend the body, and hemoglobin carries oxygen.
All of them are chains of amino acids folded into specific shapes.
w: Carbohydrates are mainly for energy and structure.
Lipids store energy, build membranes and make steroid hormones.
Nucleic acids store and use genetic information.

q: Use the table. Which macromolecule is NOT built from a single repeating type of monomer?
e: Lipids are a varied group (fats, phospholipids, steroids). Fats are built from glycerol plus fatty acids, which are not a single repeating monomer, so lipids aren't true polymers.
Carbohydrates repeat monosaccharides, proteins repeat amino acids, and nucleic acids repeat nucleotides.

q: The diagram shows sodium reacting with chlorine. What happens to form the bond?
o: Sodium transfers one electron to chlorine, making oppositely charged ions that attract.
Sodium and chlorine share one pair of electrons equally, forming a covalent bond.
Chlorine gives seven electrons to sodium, so both atoms end up with full shells.
Protons move from sodium's nucleus to chlorine's nucleus, which gives the two ions their charges.
e: Sodium has 1 electron in its outer shell; chlorine has 7. Sodium loses its outer electron (orange) and chlorine gains it.
Now Na⁺ (2, 8) and Cl⁻ (2, 8, 8) each have a full outer shell. Their opposite charges attract: that attraction is an ionic bond.
Sharing electron pairs would be a covalent bond, which forms between nonmetals. Protons never move in a chemical reaction.
w: Sharing is covalent bonding, typical of two nonmetals.
It's easier for Na to lose 1 than for Cl to lose 7.
Only electrons move in chemical reactions.

q: After the electron moves, why does the sodium ion have a positive charge?
o: It has 11 protons but only 10 electrons.
It gained a proton from chlorine.
It has more electrons than protons.
e: A neutral sodium atom has 11 protons (+) and 11 electrons (−).
After losing one electron it has 11 protons and 10 electrons, so it has one extra positive charge: Na⁺.
Chloride is the reverse: 17 protons and 18 electrons, so it is Cl⁻.
w: Protons don't move in chemical reactions.
Nuclei don't change in chemical reactions.

q: Molecule B (CO₂) has two polar C=O bonds, but the molecule as a whole is nonpolar. What explains this?
o: Its linear shape is symmetric, so the two bond dipoles cancel.
Carbon and oxygen have equal electronegativity, so electrons are shared evenly.
Lone pairs on the central carbon bend the molecule into a V shape.
It is an ionic compound made of ions, not a molecule with bonds.
e: CO₂ (B) is linear: its two C=O dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel, like two equal tug-of-war teams. (Methane, C, is nonpolar too: its C–H bonds are only very slightly polar and are arranged symmetrically.)
Water (A) and ammonia (D) have lone pairs that make them lopsided, so their bond dipoles don't cancel and the molecules are polar. That's why water dissolves salt and sugar so well.
w: O is much more electronegative than C, so each C=O bond is polar.
CO₂ has NO lone pairs on carbon; it is linear, not bent.
CO₂ is a covalent molecule made of nonmetals.

q: In the H–Cl molecule shown, why does the chlorine end carry a partial negative charge (δ−)?
o: Chlorine is more electronegative, so it pulls the shared electrons closer.
Chlorine has given its electrons to hydrogen, forming an ionic bond.
Hydrogen has more protons, so it pushes the shared electrons toward chlorine.
The electrons are shared exactly equally between the two atoms.
e: Electronegativity is an atom's pull on shared electrons. Chlorine (3.0) pulls harder than hydrogen (2.1).
The shared pair spends more time near Cl, making that end slightly negative (δ−) and the H end slightly positive (δ+). This is a POLAR covalent bond.
If the electrons were transferred completely, it would be ionic; if shared exactly equally (as in Cl–Cl), it would be nonpolar.
w: The electrons are shared unequally, not given away; HCl is covalent.
Equal sharing would give no δ+ or δ− ends.

q: When solutions of silver nitrate and sodium chloride are mixed, a white solid forms: AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl + NaNO₃. Which panel shows this type of reaction?
e: Two compounds trade partners: Ag pairs up with Cl, and Na pairs up with NO₃. That is double replacement, AB + CD → AD + CB (panel D).
The solid that forms (AgCl) is called a precipitate. Many double-replacement reactions in water make a precipitate, a gas or water.
w: A is synthesis (two things combine into one).
B is decomposition (one thing breaks apart).
C is single replacement; here both reactants are compounds.

q: What do carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14 have in common?
e: All three have atomic number 6, so all have 6 protons. That's what makes them carbon.
They differ only in neutrons (6, 7 and 8), which changes the mass number. Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons are isotopes.

q: Carbon-14 is radioactive. A bone found at a dig site has 25% of its original carbon-14 left. Based on the graph, about how old is the bone?
e: The graph halves every 5,730 years: that is carbon-14's half-life.
100% → 50% is one half-life; 50% → 25% is a second. Two half-lives = 2 × 5,730 = 11,460 years.
A common slip is to think 25% means "one-quarter of a half-life." Each half-life cuts what's LEFT in half.
w: Less than one half-life would leave more than 50%.
After one half-life, 50% is left, not 25%.

q: A person with lactose intolerance makes very little lactase. Based on the table, what happens when this person drinks milk?
o: Lactose isn't split, so it reaches the large intestine, where bacteria ferment it, causing gas and cramps.
Sucrase is also blocked, so the sucrose in sweetened foods and drinks isn't digested and causes gas and cramps.
Milk proteins aren't digested, because lactase is the enzyme that breaks down proteins like casein.
Lactose is split too fast, so extra glucose is absorbed and the person's blood sugar spikes.
e: Only monosaccharides are absorbed. Lactase normally splits lactose into glucose + galactose in the small intestine.
Without enough lactase, lactose stays whole and moves on to the large intestine. Bacteria there ferment it, making gas, and the extra sugar draws in water (bloating, diarrhea).
Lactase tablets or lactose-free milk (lactose already split) prevent this.
w: Sucrase, a different enzyme, splits sucrose; it isn't affected.
Lactase acts only on lactose, a sugar, not on proteins.
Less lactose is broken down, so LESS glucose is absorbed.

q: A competitive inhibitor has a shape similar to the substrate and binds the enzyme's active site. Based on the graph, how can its effect be overcome?
o: Add much more substrate, so substrate molecules win the active sites most of the time.
Remove most of the substrate so the inhibitor has nothing left to compete with.
Heat the enzyme far above body temperature so it binds substrate faster.
Nothing can overcome it; the maximum rate always stays lower than it is without the inhibitor.
e: The inhibitor and substrate compete for the same active site. At low substrate, the inhibitor wins often and the rate is much lower.
As substrate concentration rises, substrate molecules outnumber the inhibitor, and the dashed curve climbs toward the same maximum rate.
Many drugs work this way, for example statins block an enzyme the liver uses to make cholesterol.
w: Less substrate would make the inhibitor win even more often.
Too much heat would denature the enzyme.
The graph shows both curves approaching the same maximum.
